question: What is the sum insured?
answer: The sum insured is the maximum amount your insurer will pay for covered claims in a policy year. In health insurance it is the total cover available; in motor insurance the equivalent is the Insured Declared Value (IDV).

question: What is a deductible?
answer: A deductible is the amount you pay yourself on each claim before the insurer pays. For example, with a deductible of ₹5,000 on a home claim of ₹40,000 the insurer pays ₹35,000 (subject to policy terms).

question: What is co-payment?
answer: Co-payment (co-pay) is a fixed percentage of every admissible claim that you bear. With a 10% co-pay on a ₹1,00,000 claim, you pay ₹10,000 and the insurer pays ₹90,000.

question: What is a room rent limit?
answer: Some health policies cap the room rent you can claim per day (for example 1% of the sum insured). If you choose a costlier room, other charges may be reduced proportionately. Policies with a single private room limit or no limit avoid this.

question: What is the difference between cashless and reimbursement claims?
answer: In a cashless claim the insurer or TPA settles the bill directly with a network hospital, so you pay only non-covered items. In a reimbursement claim you pay the hospital and then submit bills and documents to the insurer to get your money back.

question: What is a network hospital?
answer: A network hospital is a hospital that has a tie-up with the insurer or its TPA for cashless treatment. Check the current network list before planned admissions.

question: What is a TPA?
answer: A Third Party Administrator (TPA) is a company licensed by IRDAI that handles health claim processing, cashless approvals and hospital coordination on behalf of the insurer.

question: What are pre- and post-hospitalization expenses?
answer: Pre-hospitalization covers medical expenses for a fixed period before admission (often 30 to 60 days) and post-hospitalization covers expenses after discharge (often 60 to 90 days), such as tests and medicines related to the same illness.

question: What is a waiting period in health insurance?
answer: A waiting period is the time after a policy starts during which certain claims are not payable. Typical ones are 30 days for illness, 1 to 2 years for specific procedures, and up to 3 or 4 years for pre-existing diseases.

question: What is a pre-existing disease (PED)?
answer: A pre-existing disease is a condition you had before buying the policy. It is usually covered only after the PED waiting period (commonly 2 to 4 years) and must be disclosed truthfully at purchase.

question: What is a family floater policy?
answer: A family floater gives one sum insured that is shared by all insured family members. Any member can use it, and a single premium is paid for the whole family. It is usually cheaper than separate individual policies.

question: Is maternity covered in health insurance?
answer: Some health policies cover maternity and newborn expenses after a waiting period (often 2 to 4 years) and up to a sub-limit. Check your policy schedule for maternity cover and limits.

question: How do I claim the Section 80D tax benefit?
answer: Premiums paid for health insurance can be claimed as a deduction under Section 80D of the Income Tax Act, up to prescribed limits, for self, family and parents. Pay by a non-cash mode and keep your premium receipt; confirm current limits with a tax adviser.

question: What is the difference between term life and whole life insurance?
answer: Term life insurance pays a sum assured to your nominee only if you die within the policy term and has low premiums. Whole life insurance covers you for your entire life and may include a savings component, at a higher premium.

question: Who is a nominee?
answer: A nominee is the person you name to receive the policy benefit if you pass away. Keep nominee details and relationship up to date. In some cases legal heirs may have a claim over the proceeds.

question: What is a grace period?
answer: A grace period is the extra time after the premium due date (usually 15 to 30 days) in which you can still pay and keep the policy in force without losing continuity benefits. Claims during the grace period may be affected, so renew early.

question: What happens if my policy lapses and can I revive it?
answer: A policy lapses when the premium is not paid by the end of the grace period and cover stops. Many insurers allow revival within a limited period on payment of the overdue premium, and sometimes fresh health declarations or medical tests.

question: What is the free-look period?
answer: After you receive a new policy you usually have 15 to 30 days (the free-look period) to review it and return it for a refund of premium, less small deductions, if you disagree with the terms.

question: What is IDV in motor insurance?
answer: Insured Declared Value (IDV) is the current market value of your vehicle set at the time of purchase or renewal. It is the maximum amount payable for total loss or theft and reduces as the vehicle ages.

question: What is a no-claim bonus (NCB)?
answer: A no-claim bonus is a discount on your own-damage premium or extra cover for each claim-free year. It is lost if you make a claim and stays with you even if you change insurer.

question: What is zero depreciation cover?
answer: Zero depreciation (nil depreciation) is a motor add-on under which the insurer pays the full cost of replaced parts without deducting depreciation, so you pay less out of pocket after an accident.

question: What is the difference between third-party and own-damage motor insurance?
answer: Third-party cover is mandatory and pays for injury or damage you cause to others. Own-damage cover pays for damage to your own vehicle from accident, fire, theft or natural calamity. A comprehensive policy includes both.

question: Is damage from a joy ride or by an unlicensed driver covered under motor insurance?
answer: Generally no. Claims are usually not payable if the vehicle was used for joy riding without the owner's consent, or if it was driven by a person without a valid driving licence. Damage caused by drunk driving is also commonly excluded.

question: What does home insurance cover?
answer: Home insurance covers damage to the structure and contents from events such as fire, flood, storms and burglary, depending on the plan. Gradual seepage, wear and tear and negligence are typically excluded.

question: What does travel insurance cover?
answer: International travel insurance can cover emergency medical expenses, trip cancellation, delayed or lost baggage, passport loss and flight delays. Check the sum insured and destination requirements such as Schengen minimums.

question: How do I update my contact details?
answer: You can update your phone number, email, city and state from the Profile page of this portal. For changes to name, date of birth or PAN, contact customer support with supporting documents.

question: How long does claim settlement take?
answer: Cashless approvals are usually decided within a few hours. Reimbursement claims are generally settled within 15 to 30 days of receiving complete documents. Delays happen when documents are pending or an investigation is needed.

question: How do I raise a grievance?
answer: First write to the insurer's grievance cell. If unresolved within 15 days, escalate on IRDAI's Bima Bharosa portal. As a last resort you can approach the Insurance Ombudsman for your region.

question: Why was my claim rejected and can I appeal?
answer: Common reasons include a lapsed policy, an excluded event, non-disclosure, missing documents or a late intimation. The rejection letter states the reason. You can send a written representation with new documents, then use the grievance process.
